nameStory: The Virginia opossum gets its name from the Virginia Colony, where European colonists first encountered this unusual marsupial in the early 1600s. The word 'opossum' comes from the Algonquian word 'aposoum,' meaning 'white animal' - a fitting name for North America's only native marsupial with its distinctive grayish-white fur.
description: The Virginia opossum is a cat-sized marsupial with a pointed snout, small dark eyes, and large naked ears. Adults typically weigh 4-14 pounds and have coarse grayish fur with white-tipped guard hairs that give them a grizzled appearance. Their most distinctive feature is a long, hairless, prehensile tail that looks like pink or gray leather and can wrap around branches.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: About the size of a house cat but with a more elongated body and shorter legs. The pointed snout is much longer than a cat's, giving them an almost rat-like face profile.

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: Long, thick, completely hairless tail that feels leathery to the touch and is prehensile like a monkey's. Often dirty or muddy-looking, it's unmistakable among New England mammals.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Coarse, grizzled grayish fur with longer white-tipped guard hairs that stick out. The undercoat feels woolly while the guard hairs are stiff and wiry. Face is usually whitish with darker ears.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Five-toed prints with the hind foot showing a distinctive thumb-like digit that sticks out at an angle. Front tracks look hand-like, while rear tracks resemble tiny human hands.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Slow-moving and clumsy on the ground, often seen shuffling along with a distinctive waddle. When threatened, they may 'play dead' by lying still with mouth open and tongue hanging out.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Scattered garbage, overturned pet food bowls, and small dark droppings about the size of a dog's but more cylindrical. Often leave muddy paw prints on garbage cans or decking.

habitat: Virginia opossums adapt to almost any habitat but prefer areas near water with abundant food sources. You'll find them in suburban neighborhoods, along wooded streams, in brushy areas, and anywhere with access to human food sources like garbage, pet food, or compost. They're excellent climbers and often den in hollow trees, abandoned burrows, or under porches and sheds.

seasonality.spring: Breeding season begins, with females carrying young in their pouches. More active as they search for mates and food after winter.
seasonality.summer: Most active season with young opossums becoming independent. Peak time for suburban encounters as they raid gardens and garbage cans.
seasonality.fall: Busy feeding season as they prepare for winter, often seen foraging for fallen fruits and persimmons. Road encounters increase as they search for food.
seasonality.winter: Less active but don't hibernate; their hairless ears and tail are susceptible to frostbite. Often seek shelter in heated spaces like garages or under houses.

funFact: Opossums have a mouth full of 50 teeth - more than any other North American mammal - and are naturally immune to snake venom, including that of rattlesnakes and copperheads!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with cats at a distance, but the long pointed snout and hairless tail are dead giveaways. Remember: if it has a naked rat-like tail, it's definitely an opossum - no other New England mammal has this feature.
contextualKnowledge: Many people call them 'possums,' which is technically correct in casual conversation, though true possums are different marsupials found in Australia. Virginia opossums are North America's only native marsupial, making them quite unique in our local fauna.
compareHints: The Virginia opossum is the only member of its genus in New England and indeed the only marsupial of any kind in the region. Its closest relatives are other opossum species found in Central and South America, but none of these occur naturally in North America north of Mexico.
